# What is buffer time? Learn how to use buffer times in scheduling

Buffer time is a powerful feature in scheduling that can help you manage your calendar more effectively. Whether you're preparing for a meeting, traveling between appointments, or taking a break to reset, buffer time ensures that your schedule runs smoothly. In this guide, we’ll cover everything you need to know about buffer time, its benefits, and how to use it to improve your productivity.

![Cal.com event settings showing the 'Limits' tab with options to set buffer time before and after events, allowing users to block time before and after appointments.](https://framerusercontent.com/images/f47e1rY68uDf3AoqJMsAC3cWv4Y.png?width=2000&height=1190)

## [What is buffer time in scheduling?](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-buffer-time-learn-how-to-use-buffer-times-in-scheduling\#what-is-buffer-time-in-scheduling)

In simple terms, buffer time refers to extra time scheduled **before or after** your meetings or appointments. This extra time is essential for several reasons, including ensuring that you have enough time to **prepare** for a meeting, **travel** between meetings, or **wrap up** effectively after a call or session.

While buffer time doesn’t affect how long it takes for an event page to load, it plays a crucial role in preventing scheduling conflicts and ensuring that your day flows smoothly. Think of buffer time as a cushion between appointments, offering you breathing room.

## [Why buffer time is important for calendar scheduling](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-buffer-time-learn-how-to-use-buffer-times-in-scheduling\#why-buffer-time-is-important-for-calendar-scheduling)

Incorporating buffer time into your schedule provides several key benefits:

1. **Prevent scheduling overlaps**

By adding buffer time before and after meetings, you ensure that your appointments don’t overlap, reducing the risk of running late or missing meetings entirely.

2. **Improve focus and productivity**

Buffer time allows you to take a quick break, gather your thoughts, or review notes. This ensures you're mentally prepared for the next meeting, enhancing your focus and productivity throughout the day.

3. **Reduce stress and avoid burnout**

A packed calendar with back-to-back meetings can be overwhelming. Buffer time provides space to **reset** before the next event, preventing mental fatigue and burnout.

4. **Enhance flexibility for unexpected tasks**

If a meeting runs longer than expected, buffer time gives you the flexibility to adjust without affecting subsequent appointments. It also allows room for unexpected tasks or delays, ensuring you can stay on top of your schedule.


## [How to set buffer time in scheduling tools](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-buffer-time-learn-how-to-use-buffer-times-in-scheduling\#how-to-set-buffer-time-in-scheduling-tools)

Setting up buffer time in **Cal.com** is quick and easy. Here are the exact steps:

1. **Log in to** [**app.cal.com**](http://app.cal.com/)

Open your browser and log in to your **Cal.com** account.

2. **Select one of your event types**

Choose the event type for which you want to add buffer time.

3. **Click on the "Limits" tab**

Navigate to the **Limits** tab within the event settings.

4. **Change the buffer time values**

Adjust the buffer time before and/or after the event by setting your preferred values.

5. **Save the event type**

Once you’ve set up the buffer time, click “Save” to apply the changes to your event type.


And that’s it! You’ve successfully set up buffer time for your event type in Cal.com.

**Removing buffer time:**

To remove buffer time from events that haven't been scheduled yet, follow the same steps but set the buffer time to ' **no buffer time'**.

## [How to use buffer time effectively in your scheduling](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-buffer-time-learn-how-to-use-buffer-times-in-scheduling\#how-to-use-buffer-time-effectively-in-your-scheduling)

To make the most out of buffer time, consider these tips for effective use:

### [1\. Customizing buffer time for different event types](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-buffer-time-learn-how-to-use-buffer-times-in-scheduling\#1-customizing-buffer-time-for-different-event-types)

Most scheduling platforms, like Cal.com, allow you to set **custom buffer times** for each event type. For example, a short one-on-one meeting might only need a 5-10 minute buffer, while a lengthy workshop or a session involving multiple participants could benefit from a 15-30 minute buffer.

### [2\. Account for travel time between appointments](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-buffer-time-learn-how-to-use-buffer-times-in-scheduling\#2-account-for-travel-time-between-appointments)

If your meetings involve travel, make sure to factor in buffer time to allow for **commuting**. Adding extra time between appointments ensures you're not rushed and have time to get to your next meeting location.

### [3\. Consider mental breaks for self-care](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-buffer-time-learn-how-to-use-buffer-times-in-scheduling\#3-consider-mental-breaks-for-self-care)

Back-to-back meetings can lead to exhaustion, especially in high-stress environments. Buffer time provides you with an opportunity to step away, refresh, and recharge mentally, ultimately improving your performance.

## [Practical applications of buffer time](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-buffer-time-learn-how-to-use-buffer-times-in-scheduling\#practical-applications-of-buffer-time)

Buffer time isn’t just a theoretical concept. Tt can have real, tangible benefits when applied in your daily schedule. Here are some practical applications and examples:

### [1\. Preparing for client meetings](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-buffer-time-learn-how-to-use-buffer-times-in-scheduling\#1-preparing-for-client-meetings)

Imagine you have a back-to-back series of meetings with clients. Without buffer time, you might feel rushed between appointments, especially if you need time to review your notes, prepare any documents, or simply mentally shift from one discussion to another.

**Practical example:**

You have a 30-minute client meeting at 10:00 AM. Without buffer time, the next meeting at 10:30 AM might start right after, leaving you no time to review notes or settle into a new conversation. By adding a 10-minute buffer before and after the meeting, you have time to wrap up the first call, take notes, and prepare for the next meeting, making you more focused and professional.

### [2\. Travel time between meetings](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-buffer-time-learn-how-to-use-buffer-times-in-scheduling\#2-travel-time-between-meetings)

If your meetings are in different locations, buffer time is essential for **traveling** between appointments. This prevents you from feeling rushed or late, which can help reduce stress and ensure you arrive at your next meeting on time.

**Practical example:**

You’re scheduling an in-person meeting with a client at your office and another with a colleague across town. You know it will take 20 minutes to travel between the locations. Adding a 20-minute buffer time ensures that you’ll be on time for both meetings and that there’s no pressure if the first meeting runs a bit over.

### [3\. Wrapping up and resetting after meetings](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-buffer-time-learn-how-to-use-buffer-times-in-scheduling\#3-wrapping-up-and-resetting-after-meetings)

It’s not just about the time before meetings. Buffer time can also help you to **reset** after a meeting, especially if it was emotionally draining or complex. Having time to reflect, jot down important notes, or even take a break between appointments can improve your performance in the next one.

**Practical example:**

You just had a 45-minute team meeting, and it was full of discussions and decisions that require follow-up actions. Instead of jumping immediately into the next meeting, you add a 10-minute buffer after the team meeting. During this time, you gather your thoughts, make quick notes, and prepare for the next conversation, ultimately improving the quality of the next meeting.

### [4\. Reducing mental fatigue in a busy day](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-buffer-time-learn-how-to-use-buffer-times-in-scheduling\#4-reducing-mental-fatigue-in-a-busy-day)

If your schedule is packed with multiple meetings, back-to-back events can lead to mental fatigue, affecting your focus and performance. Buffer time provides space to relax, recharge, and prepare for the next task with renewed energy.

**Practical example:**

You have four 30-minute client calls lined up, one after the other. Instead of scheduling them without any breaks, you add 5-10 minute buffer times between each call. This small break helps you refresh, drink some water, stretch, or take a few deep breaths, ensuring that you’re sharp and focused throughout the day.

## [Buffer time and multi-user meetings](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-buffer-time-learn-how-to-use-buffer-times-in-scheduling\#buffer-time-and-multi-user-meetings)

When scheduling multi-user meetings, buffer time can impact **availability** and the distribution of appointments. For example:

- **Round robin meetings:** If buffer times are set for different team members, it can affect the distribution of meetings among them. Ensure you balance buffer time across all participants to avoid uneven scheduling.

- **Collective events:** If one participant has buffer time set, it might block available time slots for others, affecting the overall meeting availability.


By keeping these factors in mind, you can ensure that buffer times don’t inadvertently disrupt group scheduling.

## [How buffer time works in scheduling software](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-buffer-time-learn-how-to-use-buffer-times-in-scheduling\#how-buffer-time-works-in-scheduling-software)

Buffer time is applied only to meetings booked through your scheduling tool. It works by checking your entire calendar, including non-scheduled events, to ensure there are no overlaps.

**Example:**

If you have a 30-minute meeting with a 15-minute buffer before and after, it requires a total of **60 minutes** of free time. The meeting stays 30 minutes long, but the buffer protects your availability.

## [Troubleshooting buffer time issues](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-buffer-time-learn-how-to-use-buffer-times-in-scheduling\#troubleshooting-buffer-time-issues)

Sometimes, you may encounter issues with buffer time, such as:

- **Overlapping buffers:** A buffer may overlap with an existing meeting or event.

- **Insufficient time for meeting + buffer:** If the total time (meeting + buffer) doesn’t fit within your available hours, scheduling conflicts may arise.

- **Old buffer settings:** If buffer settings are not properly cleared, they may still be applied to scheduled events, leading to errors.


## [Conclusion: Optimize your schedule with buffer time](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-buffer-time-learn-how-to-use-buffer-times-in-scheduling\#conclusion-optimize-your-schedule-with-buffer-time)

Buffer time is an essential feature for managing your calendar effectively. By setting custom buffers between meetings, you can prevent overlaps, reduce stress, and stay productive throughout the day.

Cal.com offers a seamless, user-friendly platform for scheduling appointments and meetings, and it allows you to easily customize buffer time for each event type. With Cal.com, you can effortlessly optimize your calendar, prevent scheduling conflicts, and improve your overall productivity.

Ready to streamline your scheduling? Cal.com offers flexible scheduling features, including buffer time, to help you manage appointments with ease. [Sign up now](https://cal.com/signup)!

# What is Cron?

# What is Cron?

# What is Cron?

![](https://framerusercontent.com/images/GsbVDPY7sFDrxJMoZb6QBXYU.png?width=1824&height=913)

![](https://framerusercontent.com/images/GsbVDPY7sFDrxJMoZb6QBXYU.png?width=1824&height=913)

## [**Introducing Cron**](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-cron\#introducing-cron)

Cron is a meticulously designed calendar scheduling product for professionals and teams. It supports everything from availability sharing to team overlays and multiple time zones. The application was voted the number one productivity app in 2021 and has since been acquired by Notion. This move demonstrates the productivity industry’s confidence in Cron's ability to continue innovating and improving the consumer calendar experience. As a next-generation calendar scheduling product, Cron has continued to attract attention and make waves during its development process. They have recently released Cron for iOS, giving Apple users access to its intuitive and innovative features. Despite being in beta, [Cron](https://cron.com/) is already being used by people at companies such as Figma, Loom, and Notion. It is packed with adaptive enhancements that anticipate user needs before the mouse clicks and comes with light and dark modes.

## [**Why should you use Cron with Cal.com?**](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-cron\#why-should-you-use-cron-with-cal-com)

While Cron and Cal.com are both calendar scheduling tools, they differ in terms of scope and application. Cron is a consumer calendar scheduling product, while Cal.com is a calendar scheduling infrastructure product. Cal.com can handle tasks such as round-robin scheduling, multiple availabilities, and powering a time-based marketplace. In addition, our product has features like private single-use links, [routing forms](https://app.cal.com/apps/routing-forms), and advanced video conferencing capabilities.

Our product is easy to customize since it’s open-source and developer-friendly. If you need an integration that isn’t already part of our [app store](https://cal.com/apps), building it yourself is a fairly straightforward process. By combining Cron with Cal.com, you can take advantage of the strengths of both products and set yourself up for success while saving time.

## [**How to integrate Cron and Cal.com?**](https://cal.com/blog/what-is-cron\#how-to-integrate-cron-and-cal-com)

Integrating Cron with Cal.com is a super straightforward process; all you have to do is sign up for a Cron account and then connect it to your Cal.com account via google calendar. Doing this ensures both products are aware of what the other is doing and prevents unnecessary double bookings. In addition, this also means that all meetings booked via Cal.com will show up in Cron. As you can see, using Cron and Cal.com in combination is a simple way to cover all of your calendar scheduling bases.

# Why should you add the weather to your calendar?

# Why should you add the weather to your calendar?

# Why should you add the weather to your calendar?

![](https://framerusercontent.com/images/GLiuR6ThL36TyUdT9rqYAncEes.png?width=1824&height=912)

![](https://framerusercontent.com/images/GLiuR6ThL36TyUdT9rqYAncEes.png?width=1824&height=912)

Simple products can create a butterfly effect of positive chain reactions. A watch on your wrist ensures you always have the correct time. A thermos keeps your coffee warm so you can easily access a comforting drink. A window mount thermometer lets you know precisely how nippy it is outside. All of these tools and resources work together to support you and make your personal and professional life just a little bit easier.

## [**Ordinary items with extraordinary impact**](https://cal.com/blog/why-should-you-add-the-weather-to-your-calendar\#ordinary-items-with-extraordinary-impact)

Take a look at your phone. Yes, it’s an essential tool for communication, but it’s also much more than that. It stores photos, sends reminders, acts as an alarm every morning, and has both a camera and a built-in flashlight. These seemingly utilitarian features have been compiled into a single device that saves energy and time. Cal.com is taking a similar approach to calendar scheduling by building a system that is open source, modular, and can be used by everyone.

The Cal.com [app store](https://cal.com/apps) is a space that has been developed to simplify the way people incorporate scheduling. Our users can customize their calendar scheduling toolbox by picking and choosing from an assortment of practical integrations and extensions. Each new application provides an additional avenue that can be used to gain more free time by spending less time comparing agendas and sending out appointment reminders.

## [**An app that can make a difference**](https://cal.com/blog/why-should-you-add-the-weather-to-your-calendar\#an-app-that-can-make-a-difference)

One of the most useful apps in the store is one of the simplest. [Weather in your calendar](https://cal.com/apps/weather_in_your_calendar) allows you to view the relevant forecast every time you visit your connected calendar. The app displays a 16-day forecast using data from an [OpenWeatherMap](https://openweathermap.org/). Enter your choice, and you’re good to go.

Enabling this app means that whenever you check your calendar to verify your upcoming meetings and appointments, you also get a quick bird’s eye view of the weather. Without adding any extra steps to your workflow for the day, the app quickly lets you know if you need to bundle up or grab your umbrella on your way out the door.

The weather is a mercurial creature, and its sudden changes in temperament can cost you time, especially if you’re unprepared. Enabling weather in your calendar is a small and simple action that you can take to simplify your relationship with the weather and how it affects your schedule.

# Why you should not build your own scheduling

![](https://framerusercontent.com/images/vlmcHaU7zgv152XE2iEVp4PlkU.png?width=1024&height=505)

Let's be honest, I am biased. We sell scheduling technology, but after seeing this happen over and over again I think it is important to talk about how incredibly complex scheduling is and what deep rabbit hole awaits you if your team chooses to build everything in-house.

If you don't want to use Cal.com–that's fine. Use any other vendor out there (if you're a cool person, you lemme know why but no hard feelings). **But please just don't build it in-house unless you like to suffer.**

At first glance, creating a custom calendar and scheduling tool might seem like a straightforward and cost-effective choice. You start by integrating with Google Calendar–easy. Then you look into Zoom–aight that's a bit more. You'll spend the next three weeks submitting your application to Google and Zoom's marketplaces to get proper production keys and go through hoops-and-loops to get verified. A week later your PM is asking you to check for different timezones, but what does that even mean? Do we track timezones in the browser or do people need to submit them? What if people don't know their timezone and only their city? Ok, lemme quickly build a new timezone dropdown that handles this. Wait, WTF IS DAYLIGHT SAVINGS? You wake up from a fever dream and your PM is asking you to also ship recurring meetings. In the standup call you start to sweat slightly, but you are moving forward and start reading into the Recurrence Rule (short RRule). Only moments later you find yourself reading twenty-year old iCalendar RFCs without any modern code examples. You never thought how much CalDAV would play a role in your life.

Great. You shipped the bare minimum, but your CEO is breathing down your neck because you haven't shipped a single core-business related feature yet. After all, your team is trying to build a marketplace to connect a dog owner with a dog sitter, but all you can reply is "Hey boss, I just figured out that London (Ohio) is not the same timezone as London Europe!"

Many companies have similar, likely less funny stories and they realize typically after six months that building your own scheduling is far more complicated than it initially appeared. Here’s why opting for an existing SaaS (Software as a Service) solution is a smarter move.

Remember, use **any** scheduling tool out there if you don't wanna go with Cal.com. I'm not gonna be mad at you. pinky promise. 🤞

If you made it this far, here is an AI generated list of reasons that turned my bullet point ideas into SEO-optimized text. (Don't blame me, I don't have much time lately to write blog posts because I have to support the team to fix timezone issues).

### [**Complexity and Hidden Challenges**](https://cal.com/blog/why-you-should-not-build-your-own-scheduling\#complexity-and-hidden-challenges)

**1\. Initial Simplicity, Long-term Complexity**

Building a basic calendar or scheduling system might seem easy at the start. However, as your company grows and your needs become more sophisticated, the complexity increases exponentially. Features like timezone support, [recurring events](https://cal.com/scheduling/feature/recurring-events), calendar sharing, and integration with other tools require significant time and expertise to implement correctly.

**2\. Timezones and Conflict Checking**

Handling different timezones correctly is a major challenge in itself. Ensuring that appointments and meetings are accurately scheduled across various timezones involves intricate logic and comprehensive testing. Additionally, conflict checking—ensuring that no double-bookings occur and that resources are available when needed—requires complex algorithms and real-time updates. These functionalities are critical for a reliable scheduling system but are often underestimated in terms of development effort.

**3\. Underestimating the Workload**

Many junior engineers might underestimate the amount of work required to build a fully functional calendar and scheduling system. What starts as a seemingly simple project can quickly balloon into a complex undertaking. The initial enthusiasm can fade as they encounter the numerous edge cases and nuances involved in creating a reliable and efficient system. This underestimation can lead to project delays, increased costs, and frustration.

**4\. Maintenance and Updates**

Creating the software is just the beginning. Ongoing maintenance, updates, and bug fixes are continuous efforts that demand time and resources. A dedicated team is required to keep the system running smoothly, handle user requests, and ensure security, which diverts focus from your core business.

### [**Benefits of Off-the-Shelf SaaS Solutions**](https://cal.com/blog/why-you-should-not-build-your-own-scheduling\#benefits-of-off-the-shelf-saas-solutions)

**1\. Cost-Effective**

Using an existing SaaS solution is often cheaper than building your own. SaaS providers spread their development and maintenance costs across many users, allowing them to offer robust features at a fraction of the cost it would take to build them in-house.

**2\. Time-Saving**

With SaaS, you can be up and running in a matter of hours or days, compared to the months it might take to develop your own solution. This rapid deployment means you can focus on what matters most—growing your business.

**3\. Expert Support and Continuous Improvement**

SaaS providers specialize in their field and continuously improve their products based on user feedback and technological advancements. They offer customer support to help you navigate any issues, ensuring you always have access to the latest features and security updates.

**4\. Seamless Integration**

Most SaaS calendar and scheduling tools are designed to integrate seamlessly with other popular software your company might already be using, such as email clients, CRM systems, and project management tools. This integration enhances productivity and streamlines workflows.

**5\. Reliability and Security**

Reputable SaaS providers prioritize reliability and security. They employ teams of experts to ensure their systems are robust, secure, and compliant with industry standards, giving you peace of mind and protecting your company’s data.

### [**Real-World Example**](https://cal.com/blog/why-you-should-not-build-your-own-scheduling\#real-world-example)

Many companies that initially opt to build their own scheduling software often find themselves overwhelmed after a few months. They encounter unforeseen challenges and complexities that strain their resources and delay other important projects. Eventually, they turn to SaaS solutions to regain their footing and realize the significant benefits they offer.

### [**Focus on Your Core Business**](https://cal.com/blog/why-you-should-not-build-your-own-scheduling\#focus-on-your-core-business)

Just as you wouldn’t rebuild Stripe.com to handle your payments, you shouldn’t try to recreate a dedicated scheduling tool from scratch. Stripe has mastered the complexities of payment processing, allowing businesses to focus on their main goals without worrying about the intricate details of transactions. Similarly, using a specialized scheduling SaaS solution lets you avoid the headaches of calendar management, conflict checking, and timezone issues. By leveraging these expert tools, you can dedicate your energy and resources to what truly matters—growing and enhancing your core business.

### [**Conclusion**](https://cal.com/blog/why-you-should-not-build-your-own-scheduling\#conclusion)

While the idea of building your own calendar and scheduling software may be tempting, it’s important to recognize the hidden complexities and long-term costs involved. Opting for an off-the-shelf SaaS solution can save your company time, money, and headaches, allowing you to focus on your core business objectives. Embrace the expertise and efficiency of SaaS providers to enhance your scheduling capabilities and drive your business forward.

# Zencal vs. Calendly: Branding and Analytics Compared

Scheduling tools have become essential for managing appointments in today’s business landscape.

![Online scheduling tools used with a tablet calendar and open notebook beside a cup of coffee](https://framerusercontent.com/images/1ShOoVr3eY05IdGRXI6ApQUfUM.webp?width=1536&height=1024)

Scheduling tools have become essential for managing appointments in today’s business landscape. Among the [best scheduling software](https://cal.com/) available, Calendly has long been a leading name, simplifying meeting bookings for millions of users. Recently, newer competitors have emerged in the same space. One such contender is Zencal, a platform positioning itself as a powerful alternative. This article presents a comprehensive comparison of ZenCal vs. Calendly, focusing on their appointment branding features and analytics capabilities. We will examine how each platform handles customization and data insights, and help you determine which tool aligns better with your needs.

## [Calendly Overview](https://cal.com/blog/zencal-vs-calendly-branding-and-analytics-compared\#calendly-overview)

Calendly is one of the most popular calendar scheduling apps, known for its ease of use and broad adoption. Launched in 2013, it quickly became a go-to calendar booking platform for individuals and organizations to eliminate the back-and-forth of finding meeting times. The platform integrates with Google and Outlook calendars, automates reminders, and supports a range of meeting types. [Calendly’s user base](http://explodingtopics.com/) has grown tremendously – by late 2023, it surpassed 20 million users across 100,000+ businesses. This widespread use is a testament to its reliability and the value it provides as an [online booking system for businesses](https://cal.com/enterprise) of all sizes.

Their core offering centers on a clean scheduling experience: users create booking links for different meeting types, set their availability, and invitees self-schedule at a time that suits both parties. The platform is often cited among the best meeting schedulers because it streamlines appointment setting and integrates with many workplace tools. It offers a free tier with basic functionality and several paid plans that unlock more advanced features, which we will discuss later. It provides a robust foundation of scheduling features that have made it a staple solution for sales teams, recruiters, client consultations, and more.

## [Zencal Overview](https://cal.com/blog/zencal-vs-calendly-branding-and-analytics-compared\#zencal-overview)

Zencal is a newer entrant in the scheduling software arena, designed to compete directly with established players like Calendly. It brands itself as an all-in-one scheduling and meeting management tool, with particular emphasis on customization and analytics. It enables users to create fully branded booking pages, manage client contacts, accept payments for appointments, and track meeting metrics. Zencal’s appeal lies in offering capabilities beyond simple scheduling – for example, it lets users employ their own branding and even generate advanced reports on meetings. By including features like client management, revenue tracking from paid meetings, and post-meeting feedback collection, it blurs the line between a scheduler and a lightweight CRM. It is positioned as an online booking system for businesses that want to optimize their scheduling process and “book more meetings” with less effort. Zencal offers a generous free plan (with most features enabled) and affordable paid plans for power users. As we compare it to Calendly, we’ll see that Zencal’s focus on customization and data insights caters to users who need more than the basics. Next, let’s dive into how each platform handles branding and user experience customization on its scheduling pages.

![Top scheduling tools represented by a hand writing in a May 2021 desk calendar beside coffee and stationery](https://framerusercontent.com/images/XRkab8mF3EUrqXO8h36QvWdBU.webp?width=1536&height=1024)

## [Branding and Customization Features](https://cal.com/blog/zencal-vs-calendly-branding-and-analytics-compared\#branding-and-customization-features)

For companies and professionals, maintaining a consistent brand image during the scheduling process can be important. Calendly and Zencal both recognize this need, but they approach customization differently.

In Calendly’s paid plans, users can add their company logo, adjust color themes, and create custom invitee questions to align the scheduling page with their brand. Teams and Professional tiers allow removing Calendly’s own logo and name from the booking pages, offering a semi-white-label experience. For example, on the Standard (Professional) plan and above. There is no native support for using a custom domain on Calendly’s hosted scheduling pages. In practice, this means small businesses using the free version must accept Calendly’s logo/link on their scheduling page, while paid subscribers can present a more white-labeled interface.

Zencal was built with branding in mind, enabling extensive customization even for free users. You can upload your own logo and cover image to your booking pages, set custom colors to match your brand palette, and personalize the styling. Notably, it allows you to remove all branding from your scheduling pages. This means a user can share a booking link that looks and feels like their own website, providing a fully branded experience to clients. It also supports embedding the scheduler on your own site with an inline frame or pop-up, and it provides options to customize confirmation pages and email notifications with your branding. While Calendly offers many of these features only in paid plans, Zencal includes them by default, which is a significant draw for users who prioritize branding.

## [Analytics and Reporting](https://cal.com/blog/zencal-vs-calendly-branding-and-analytics-compared\#analytics-and-reporting)

Beyond booking a meeting, booking platform analytics and reporting tools can provide insight into your scheduling patterns, popular meeting times, team performance, and more. Historically, Calendly’s reporting in lower-tier plans was limited – users could view basic metrics, such as the number of meetings scheduled, but comprehensive in-app analytics were lacking. However, in 2023, it introduced a new Analytics dashboard for team accounts to offer deeper insights. This tool provides an intuitive dashboard with key metrics: you can see popular meeting days and times, your top schedulers or “power users,” and the most frequently booked event types, among other data points. Admins on a team plan can view organization-wide stats, while individual users can access their personal scheduling stats.

Calendly’s analytics allow filtering by date range, team, user, and meeting type, helping managers understand scheduling trends and optimize workflows. It supports tracking conversions by integrating with Google Analytics and Meta Pixel as well. For example, a marketing team could embed a Calendly booking widget on a landing page and use Google Analytics to track how many visitors convert into scheduled meetings.

Zencal has emphasized this as a core feature. On the platform, users can generate reports on their meetings and clients without needing external tools. Zencal’s dashboard tracks metrics such as the number of bookings over time, attendance rates, and revenue earned from paid meetings. Because it includes a client management component, you can view a client’s history and total spending on your services in one place. For teams, it offers team-level analytics as well – managers can see how meetings are distributed among team members and identify productivity trends. The platform also supports integration with Google Analytics and Facebook Pixel by allowing UTM parameters and tracking code on booking pages, so you can monitor traffic sources and conversion rates for bookings. Users who consider data insight a priority may appreciate that Zencal surfaces such analytics in-app without requiring the highest tier plan. It positions itself as not just a scheduler but one of the scheduling analytics tools that help improve your appointment strategy over time.

## [Pricing and Plans](https://cal.com/blog/zencal-vs-calendly-branding-and-analytics-compared\#pricing-and-plans)

When choosing a scheduling app, cost and plan limitations are essential factors, especially for freelancers or small businesses on a budget. Let’s compare Calendly pricing and Zencastr’s pricing, and how their free tiers stack up.

- **Calendly Pricing:** Calendly offers a free plan that allows one active event type per user and basic features. This free version is suitable for individual use or very simple needs, but it’s limited – for instance, you cannot create multiple different appointment types simultaneously without upgrading. Paid plans include the Essentials/Standard plan, which adds unlimited event types, integrations with tools like Zoom and Slack, custom branding, and the ability to remove its branding. Above that, the Professional/Teams plan includes team features like round-robin events, pooled availability for team scheduling, and advanced analytics dashboards. Calendly also has an Enterprise plan (custom pricing starting at several thousand dollars per year) for large organizations needing SSO, security audits, and dedicated support.

- **Zencal Pricing:** The platform proclaims that if your meetings are unpaid, you can likely use Zencal for free indefinitely. The free plan places very few restrictions. In fact, almost all features are available without charge. The only things reserved for paid plans are the ability to accept online payments for bookings and advanced team management capabilities. In other words, it doesn’t limit core scheduling features in the free tier; you only need to upgrade if you require the e-commerce aspect (selling paid meetings or packages) or if you are running a team account with multiple collaborators. Zencal’s paid plans are also competitively priced: for instance, a Pro plan is around $15/month (with discounts for annual billing), which allows collecting payments and may support larger teams. There is also a Team plan charged per user, which remains in a similar range or lower than Calendly’s equivalent team tier. The emphasis is that it aims to offer more value at a lower cost per user.


Both tools offer good value in different ways: Calendly for its proven platform and extensive integration ecosystem, and Zencal for its feature-rich free plan and affordable upgrades.

![Meeting scheduler apps shown on a smartphone with a weekly task management interface](https://framerusercontent.com/images/Ilp4b2ghyTYrfWaqTSvkvbD0cA.webp?width=1536&height=1024)

## [Use Cases: Small Business vs. Team Needs](https://cal.com/blog/zencal-vs-calendly-branding-and-analytics-compared\#use-cases-small-business-vs-team-needs)

For a [scheduling app for small businesses](https://app.cal.com/signup) or solo entrepreneurs, Zencal holds a lot of appeals. These users often need an affordable solution that still looks professional and provides the necessary functionality. Its ability to provide virtually all features in its free version is a strong advantage for a budget-conscious small business. A solo consultant, for example, can use Zencal to offer a variety of meeting options to clients, all branded with their own logo and style, without paying monthly fees. Additionally, suppose that the consultant decides to charge for sessions. In that case, Zencal has built-in payment integration (available on its Pro plan) with support for coupons and tracking client purchase history – effectively turning the scheduler into a lightweight e-commerce booking system.

Calendly, on the other hand, is often favored by mid-sized and larger teams in corporate environments. For team scheduling apps where multiple employees or departments coordinate meetings, its mature ecosystem and enterprise features can be crucial. Teams benefit from its polished scheduling workflows, like round-robin assignment and pooled availability. Calendly also offers admin controls to enforce certain settings across an organization and ensure consistent use of the tool. The new analytics dashboards are particularly useful for managers to monitor team performance.

Moreover, its extensive integration options with corporate systems make it attractive to businesses that want scheduling to seamlessly fit into their existing toolchain. While a small business can certainly use Calendly – and many do, happily – the platform’s tiered pricing and feature set are clearly designed to scale up to enterprise needs. In contrast, Zencal is still growing its integration list and focusing on core scheduling enhancements, which may be perfectly fine for a small operation but could be a consideration for a larger company with complex requirements.

## [Potential Disadvantages of Zencal and Calendly](https://cal.com/blog/zencal-vs-calendly-branding-and-analytics-compared\#potential-disadvantages-of-zencal-and-calendly)

While Zencal and Calendly are both popular choices for scheduling and appointment management, each platform comes with its own set of limitations that users should consider before making a decision. One common drawback for both tools is the restriction placed on free plans. Calendly, for instance, limits free users to a single active event type and restricts access to advanced integrations and customization features. This can be frustrating for individuals or small businesses who need more flexibility without committing to a paid subscription. Zencal, while more generous with its free tier, still reserves some critical features—such as accepting online payments and advanced team management—for its paid plans. Users who require these capabilities may find themselves needing to upgrade sooner than expected.

Another limitation is the learning curve associated with each tool. Although both Zencal and Calendly are designed to be user-friendly, new users may encounter challenges when navigating advanced settings or customizing their booking pages. For example, configuring integrations or setting up team scheduling features can be less intuitive, especially for those without prior experience with scheduling software. This initial complexity may slow down onboarding for organizations or individuals looking for a quick setup. Integration limitations also present a challenge. While Calendly boasts a robust set of integrations with popular tools like Google Calendar, Zoom, and Slack, it may not support more niche or less common platforms that some businesses rely on. Zencal integrates well with major calendar services but may lack the breadth of third-party integrations that larger organizations require. This can hinder workflow automation and force users to seek workarounds or additional tools.

Both platforms are also dependent on a stable internet connection, as they are web-based applications. In areas with unreliable connectivity, this reliance can disrupt scheduling operations and lead to missed appointments or notifications. Additionally, privacy concerns may arise, particularly with Calendly, as sharing availability links publicly could expose sensitive information about user schedules. Some users are uncomfortable with this level of transparency, especially when dealing with external clients or partners.

Cal.com emerges as a strong alternative for users who find these limitations restrictive. As an open-source platform, it offers greater flexibility and control. Users can self-host the software, ensuring data privacy and the ability to customize the platform extensively. This makes Cal.com especially attractive to organizations with unique requirements or heightened privacy concerns. By addressing the shortcomings of both Zencal and Calendly, it provides a compelling solution for those seeking a more adaptable and privacy-focused scheduling tool.

## [Other Alternatives](https://cal.com/blog/zencal-vs-calendly-branding-and-analytics-compared\#other-alternatives)

A particularly notable alternative is [Cal.com](https://cal.com/), an open-source scheduling platform that has garnered attention as a flexible, developer-friendly solution. Unlike Calendly and Zencal, which are proprietary services, [Cal.com](https://cal.com/) offers its code openly, allowing organizations to self-host their own scheduling system or customize it extensively. This means companies can effectively download scheduling software (or deploy it to their servers) to have full control over data and branding. Its open-source nature makes it extremely customizable – in fact, it’s often praised for allowing deeper modifications not just to appearance but to core functionality. For example, businesses with in-house developers can add unique features or integrations on top of it that might not be possible with a closed platform. This alternative also supports custom domains out of the box and truly white-label experiences since you’re running your own instance if you choose.

It also offers a hosted version with pricing similar to its competitors, aiming to provide a balance of convenience and flexibility. Some users choose [Cal.com](https://cal.com/) over Calendly because they felt they were paying for features in Calendly they didn’t need, whereas its free version already includes key capabilities like multiple calendar connections and Google Analytics integration. Acuity Scheduling is known for appointment scheduling with advanced calendar management and is popular with wellness businesses. [YouCanBook.me](https://cal.com/) focuses on providing a personalized booking page linked to your calendar and has been recognized for its flexibility in tailoring booking forms.

![Calendar scheduling in a planner with colorful sticky notes and handwritten reminders at an office desk](https://framerusercontent.com/images/0AIpuCfXFGPNwGXQDaP7psfneKo.webp?width=1536&height=1024)

Choosing between Calendly and Zencal ultimately comes down to your specific needs and preferences. Both are among the best appointment booking apps that can save you time and eliminate the hassles of manual scheduling. If you value a tried-and-true platform with extensive integrations and you’re working with larger teams or corporate settings, Calendly’s polished experience and advanced team features make it a safe bet. These calendar booking solutions enable you to present clients with a branded scheduling page and gather useful data on your meeting trends without requiring extra tools or incurring hefty fees.

# Zoho Calendar Now Works with Cal.com!

# Zoho Calendar Now Works with Cal.com!

# Zoho Calendar Now Works with Cal.com!

![](https://framerusercontent.com/images/qzYTktuHXwK0YieXZ1GKZsW6s8.webp?width=1828&height=926)

![](https://framerusercontent.com/images/qzYTktuHXwK0YieXZ1GKZsW6s8.webp?width=1828&height=926)

## [Calendar scheduling that makes a difference](https://cal.com/blog/zoho-calendar-now-works-with-cal-com\#calendar-scheduling-that-makes-a-difference)

Cal.com was built with a simple idea: calendar scheduling infrastructure should be available to everyone. To do this we had to ask ourselves a few questions: starting with what would that look like? And more importantly, what would it feel like?  We knew that whatever solution we came up with needed to be customizable. It had to be easy to use, and most importantly, it had to be ahead of the curve. These were the priorities that acted as the spokes of the wheel upon which Cal.com was built.

Many of these challenges and issues were addressed by choosing to create an open-source product. Doing this meant that Cal.com was uniquely situated to develop and grow at an exponential rate while maintaining transparency and accountability. One of the key things that we focus on at Cal.com is iterative improvement. This, for us, means that we make changes that make sense. An agile approach allows us to scale up or roll back aspects of features in order to optimize our users' Cal.com experience. You might have noticed that our [app store](https://cal.com/resources/feature/app-store)  has been changing as we add, remove, and reorganize integration options. A great example of this is our expanded support for Zoho Calendar.

We know how much people love Zoho's suite of products, so it made sense for us to expand our options by adding an app for Zoho. This means that you can now connect your Zoho calendar to your Cal.com profile with just a few mouse clicks. This is great because it means that you can use our robust and flexible appointment setting infrastructure without having to compromise and perhaps use a digital calendar that you love a little less than Zoho.

## [Installation](https://cal.com/blog/zoho-calendar-now-works-with-cal-com\#installation)

- Sign in to your Cal.com account.

- Click on the tab labeled Apps.

- Select the Calendar category from the list of available ones within the app.

- Scroll until you see the Zoho app.

- Click Install.

- You will now be redirected to a new page and prompted to sign into your Zoho account.

- Follow the on-screen prompts in order to finalize the process.

- Once this is done, you can double-check to make sure that Zoho is properly connected by visiting your Cal.com profile and viewing the list of connected calendars.


Using Cal.com with Zoho is a great way to supercharge your workflow while still doing things your own way. Cal.com and Zoho will work together to make sure that finding a time to brainstorm and meet is a breeze, while you focus on finishing your latest presentation, pitch deck, or Ted Talk. If you want to test out our service today, just use the link below to sign up for a free account. Happy scheduling!

## [​](https://cal.com/docs/developing/introduction\#welcome-to-the-cal-com-documentation)  Welcome to the Cal.com Documentation!

This is the documentation for Cal.com, an open source scheduling platform that enables you to take bookings on your own terms. Set your availability, connect your favourite calendar and video conferencing platforms, and share your link. It’s that simple.It covers everything from setup to usage and development. Here you can explore advice and explanations for all of our features, as well as discover new tips and tricks to get the most out of the Cal.com software. This also includes the more advanced documentation covering how to build on top of Cal.com both in the codebase, by API and more. These guides will go into depth on how you can best integrate and extend Cal.com for your needs.

## Creates a new attendee - Cal.com Docs

[Developing](https://cal.com/docs/developing/introduction) [Self Hosting](https://cal.com/docs/self-hosting/installation) [Platform](https://cal.com/docs/platform/introduction) [API v2 Reference](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/introduction) [API v1 Reference](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/introduction)

Edit an existing booking

cURL

Copy

Ask AI

```
curl --request PATCH \
  --url https://api.cal.com/v1/bookings/{id} \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
  "title": "Debugging between Syed Ali Shahbaz and Hello Hello",
  "start": "2023-05-24T13:00:00.000Z",
  "end": "2023-05-24T13:30:00.000Z",
  "status": "CANCELLED"
}'
```

200

400

401

Copy

Ask AI

```
{
  "booking": {
    "id": 11223344,
    "userId": 182,
    "description": null,
    "eventTypeId": 2323232,
    "uid": "stoSJtnh83PEL4rZmqdHe2",
    "title": "Debugging between Syed Ali Shahbaz and Hello Hello",
    "startTime": "2023-05-24T13:00:00.000Z",
    "endTime": "2023-05-24T13:30:00.000Z",
    "metadata": {},
    "status": "CANCELLED",
    "responses": {
      "email": "john.doe@example.com",
      "name": "John Doe",
      "location": {
        "optionValue": "",
        "value": "inPerson"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

#### Authorizations

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/bookings/edit-an-existing-booking#authorization-api-key)

apiKey

string

query

required

#### Path Parameters

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/bookings/edit-an-existing-booking#parameter-id)

id

integer

required

ID of the booking to edit

#### Query Parameters

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/bookings/edit-an-existing-booking#parameter-api-key)

apiKey

string

required

Your API key

#### Body

application/json

Edit an existing booking related to one of your event-types

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/bookings/edit-an-existing-booking#body-title)

title

string

Booking event title

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/bookings/edit-an-existing-booking#body-start)

start

string<date-time>

Start time of the Event

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/bookings/edit-an-existing-booking#body-end)

end

string<date-time>

End time of the Event

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/bookings/edit-an-existing-booking#body-status)

status

string

Acceptable values one of \["ACCEPTED", "PENDING", "CANCELLED", "REJECTED"\]

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/bookings/edit-an-existing-booking#body-description)

description

string

Description of the meeting

#### Response

200

application/json

OK, booking edited successfully

The response is of type `any`.

## Errors - Cal.com Docs

> **Source:** https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/errors

[Skip to main content](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/errors#content-area)

[Cal.com Docs home page![light logo](https://cal.com/calcom-docs.svg)![dark logo](https://cal.com/calcom-docs-light.svg)](https://cal.com/docs)

Search...

Ctrl K

Search...

Navigation

Getting Started

Errors

[Developing](https://cal.com/docs/developing/introduction) [Self Hosting](https://cal.com/docs/self-hosting/installation) [Platform](https://cal.com/docs/platform/introduction) [API v2 Reference](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/introduction) [API v1 Reference](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/introduction)

Cal.com uses conventional HTTP response codes to indicate the success or failure of an API request. In general: Codes in the 2xx range indicate success. Codes in the 4xx range indicate an error that failed given the information provided (e.g., a required parameter was omitted, or something else failed, etc.). Codes in the 5xx range indicate an error with Cal.com’s servers (these are rare).

| HTTP | Status Code | Summary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 200 | OK | Everything worked as expected |
| 400 | Bad Request | The request was unacceptable, often due to missing a required parameter |
| 401 | Unauthorized | No valid API key provided. |
| 402 | Request Failed | The parameters were valid but the request failed. |
| 403 | Forbidden | The API key doesn’t have permissions to perform the request. |
| 404 | Not Found | The requested resource doesn’t exist. |
| 429 | Too Many Requests | Too many requests hit the API too quickly. We recommend an exponential backoff of your requests. |
| 500, 502, 503, 504 | erver Errors | Something went wrong on our servers end. (These are rare.) |

YesNo

Getting Started

Quick start

[Developing](https://cal.com/docs/developing/introduction) [Self Hosting](https://cal.com/docs/self-hosting/installation) [Platform](https://cal.com/docs/platform/introduction) [API v2 Reference](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/introduction) [API v1 Reference](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/introduction)

On this page

- [Get your API keys](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/introduction#get-your-api-keys)
- [Install the library](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/introduction#install-the-library)
- [Make your first request](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/introduction#make-your-first-request)
- [Try our Postman Collection](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/introduction#try-our-postman-collection)

## [​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/introduction\#get-your-api-keys)  Get your API keys

Your API requests are authenticated using API keys. Any request that doesn’t include an API key will return an error.You can generate an API key from **Settings >** [**Security**](https://app.cal.com/settings/security) within the application. There you will find the API keys section which allows you to generate a key for use.More information on this can be found in the [Authentication](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/authentication) page.

## [​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/introduction\#install-the-library)  Install the library

The best way to interact with our API is using a good HTTP client like **axios**:

- Node

- Python


Copy

Ask AI

```
# Install via NPM
npm install --save axios

# Install via Yarn
yarn add axios

```

## [​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/introduction\#make-your-first-request)  Make your first request

To make your first request, send an authenticated request to the event-types endpoint. This will list all of your event types.Example using `curl`:

- Curl


Copy

Ask AI

```
curl https://api.cal.com/v1/event-types?apiKey=cal_test_xxxxxx

```

## [​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/introduction\#try-our-postman-collection)  Try our Postman Collection

We’ve created a small collection of frequently made API calls that you can try in our [Postman Collection](https://www.postman.com/calcom/workspace/cd670dd8-b36d-4aee-8ab2-9044122e30d1/collection/20666831-b92a1d73-bfcc-4a5f-9ef5-cb117d49c904)

apiKey

string

query

required

#### Path Parameters

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/webhooks/edit-an-existing-webhook#parameter-id)

id

integer

required

Numeric ID of the webhook to edit

#### Query Parameters

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/webhooks/edit-an-existing-webhook#parameter-api-key)

apiKey

string

required

Your API key

#### Body

application/json

Edit an existing webhook

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/webhooks/edit-an-existing-webhook#body-subscriber-url)

subscriberUrl

string<uri>

The URL to subscribe to this webhook

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/webhooks/edit-an-existing-webhook#body-event-triggers)

eventTriggers

enum<string>

The events which should trigger this webhook call

Available options:

`BOOKING_CREATED`,

`BOOKING_RESCHEDULED`,

`BOOKING_CANCELLED`,

`MEETING_ENDED`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/webhooks/edit-an-existing-webhook#body-active)

active

boolean

Whether the webhook is active and should trigger on associated trigger events

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/webhooks/edit-an-existing-webhook#body-payload-template)

payloadTemplate

string

The template of the webhook's payload

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/webhooks/edit-an-existing-webhook#body-event-type-id)

eventTypeId

number

The event type ID if this webhook should be associated with only that event type

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v1/webhooks/edit-an-existing-webhook#body-secret)

secret

string

The secret to verify the authenticity of the received payload

#### Response

201

OK, webhook edited successfully

#### Headers

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/api-keys/refresh-api-key#parameter-authorization)

Authorization

string

required

value must be `Bearer <token>` where `<token>` is api key prefixed with cal\_

#### Body

application/json

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/api-keys/refresh-api-key#body-api-key-days-valid)

apiKeyDaysValid

number

default:30

For how many days is managed organization api key valid. Defaults to 30 days.

Required range: `x >= 1`

Example:

`60`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/api-keys/refresh-api-key#body-api-key-never-expires)

apiKeyNeverExpires

boolean

If true, organization api key never expires.

Example:

`true`

#### Response

200 - application/json

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/api-keys/refresh-api-key#response-status)

status

enum<string>

required

Available options:

`success`,

`error`

Example:

`"success"`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/api-keys/refresh-api-key#response-data)

data

object

required

Show child attributes

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/api-keys/refresh-api-key#response-data-api-key)

data.apiKey

string

required

## Create a booking - Cal.com Docs

> **Source:** https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/bookings/create-a-booking

> **Description:** 
      POST /v2/bookings is used to create regular bookings, recurring bookings and instant bookings. The request bodies for all 3 are almost the same except:
      If eventTypeId in the request body is id of a regular event, then regular booking is created.

      If it is an id of a recurring event type, then recurring booking is created.

      Meaning that the request bodies are equal but the outcome depends on what kind of event type it is with the goal of making it as seamless for developers as possible.

      For team event types it is possible to create instant meeting. To do that just pass `"instant": true` to the request body.

      The start needs to be in UTC aka if the timezone is GMT+2 in Rome and meeting should start at 11, then UTC time should have hours 09:00 aka without time zone.

      Finally, there are 2 ways to book an event type belonging to an individual user:
      1. Provide `eventTypeId` in the request body.
      2. Provide `eventTypeSlug` and `username` and optionally `organizationSlug` if the user with the username is within an organization.

      And 2 ways to book and event type belonging to a team:
      1. Provide `eventTypeId` in the request body.
      2. Provide `eventTypeSlug` and `teamSlug` and optionally `organizationSlug` if the team with the teamSlug is within an organization.

      If you are creating a seated booking for an event type with 'show attendees' disabled, then to retrieve attendees in the response either set 'show attendees' to true on event type level or
      you have to provide an authentication method of event type owner, host, team admin or owner or org admin or owner.

## Get a booking - Cal.com Docs

> **Source:** https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/bookings/get-a-booking

> **Description:** `:bookingUid` can be

      1. uid of a normal booking

      2. uid of one of the recurring booking recurrences

      3. uid of recurring booking which will return an array of all recurring booking recurrences (stored as recurringBookingUid on one of the individual recurrences).
      
      If you are fetching a seated booking for an event type with 'show attendees' disabled, then to retrieve attendees in the response either set 'show attendees' to true on event type level or
      you have to provide an authentication method of event type owner, host, team admin or owner or org admin or owner.

#### Headers

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/bookings/get-all-bookings#parameter-cal-api-version)

cal-api-version

string

default:2024-08-13

required

Must be set to 2024-08-13

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/bookings/get-all-bookings#parameter-authorization)

Authorization

string

required

value must be `Bearer <token>` where `<token>` is api key prefixed with cal\_ or managed user access token

#### Query Parameters

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/bookings/get-all-bookings#parameter-status)

status

enum<string>\[\]

Filter bookings by status. If you want to filter by multiple statuses, separate them with a comma.

Show child attributes

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/bookings/get-all-bookings#parameter)

enum<string>

Available options:

`upcoming`,

`recurring`,

`past`,

`cancelled`,

`unconfirmed`

Example:

`"?status=upcoming,past"`

string

string

string

`"?eventTypeIds=100,200"`

eventTypeId

string

#### Headers

string

string

For platform customers - OAuth client ID

#### Path Parameters

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/bookings/reschedule-a-booking#parameter-booking-uid)

bookingUid

string

required

#### Body

application/json

Accepts different types of reschedule booking input: Reschedule Booking (Option 1) or Reschedule Seated Booking (Option 2).

```
If you are rescheduling a seated booking for an event type with 'show attendees' disabled, then to retrieve attendees in the response either set 'show attendees' to true on event type level or
  you have to provide an authentication method of event type owner, host, team admin or owner or org admin or owner.
```

- Option 1

- Option 2


[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/bookings/reschedule-a-booking#body-start)

start

string

required

Start time in ISO 8601 format for the new booking

Example:

`"2024-08-13T10:00:00Z"`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/bookings/reschedule-a-booking#body-rescheduled-by)

rescheduledBy

string

Email of the person who is rescheduling the booking - only needed when rescheduling a booking that requires a confirmation.
If event type owner email is provided then rescheduled booking will be automatically confirmed. If attendee email or no email is passed then the event type
owner will have to confirm the rescheduled booking.

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/bookings/reschedule-a-booking#body-rescheduling-reason)

reschedulingReason

string

Reason for rescheduling the booking

Example:

`"User requested reschedule"`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/bookings/reschedule-a-booking#body-email-verification-code)

emailVerificationCode

string

Email verification code required when event type has email verification enabled.

Example:

`"123456"`

```
curl --request GET \

  --header 'Authorization: <authorization>'
```

#### Headers

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/cal-unified-calendars/get-meeting-details-from-calendar#parameter-authorization)

Authorization

string

required

value must be `Bearer <token>` where `<token>` is api key prefixed with cal\_ or managed user access token

#### Path Parameters

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/cal-unified-calendars/get-meeting-details-from-calendar#parameter-calendar)

calendar

enum<string>

required

Available options:

`google`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/cal-unified-calendars/get-meeting-details-from-calendar#parameter-event-uid)

eventUid

string

required

The Google Calendar event ID. You can retrieve this by getting booking references from the following endpoints:

- For team events: [https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/orgs-teams-bookings/get-booking-references-for-a-booking](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/orgs-teams-bookings/get-booking-references-for-a-booking)

- For user events: [https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/bookings/get-booking-references-for-a-booking](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/bookings/get-booking-references-for-a-booking)


#### Response

200 - application/json

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/cal-unified-calendars/get-meeting-details-from-calendar#response-status)

status

enum<string>

required

Available options:

`success`,

`error`

Example:

`"success"`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/cal-unified-calendars/get-meeting-details-from-calendar#response-data)

data

object

required

Show child attributes

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/cal-unified-calendars/get-meeting-details-from-calendar#response-data-start)

data.start

object

required

Start date and time of the calendar event with timezone information

Show child attributes

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/cal-unified-calendars/get-meeting-details-from-calendar#response-data-end)

data.end

object

required

End date and time of the calendar event with timezone information

Show child attributes

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/cal-unified-calendars/get-meeting-details-from-calendar#response-data-id)

data.id

string

required

Unique identifier of the calendar event

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/cal-unified-calendars/get-meeting-details-from-calendar#response-data-title)

data.title

string

required

Title of the calendar event

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/cal-unified-calendars/get-meeting-details-from-calendar#response-data-source)

data.source

enum<string>

required

Calendar integration source (e.g., Google Calendar, Office 365, Apple Calendar). Currently only Google Calendar is supported.

Available options:

`google`,

`office365`,

`apple`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/cal-unified-calendars/get-meeting-details-from-calendar#response-data-description)

data.description

string \| null

Detailed description of the calendar event

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/cal-unified-calendars/get-meeting-details-from-calendar#response-data-locations)

data.locations

object\[\] \| null

Conference locations with entry points (video, phone, sip, more)

- Option 1

- Option 2

- Option 3

- Option 4


Show child attributes

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/cal-unified-calendars/get-meeting-details-from-calendar#response-data-attendees)

data.attendees

object\[\] \| null

List of attendees with their response status

Show child attributes

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/cal-unified-calendars/get-meeting-details-from-calendar#response-data-status)

data.status

enum<string>

Status of the event (accepted, pending, declined, cancelled)

Available options:

`accepted`,

`pending`,

`declined`,

`cancelled`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/cal-unified-calendars/get-meeting-details-from-calendar#response-data-hosts)

data.hosts

object\[\] \| null

Information about the event hosts (organizers)

Show child attributes

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/cal-unified-calendars/get-meeting-details-from-calendar#response-data-calendar-event-owner)

data.calendarEventOwner

object

The calendar account that owns this event. This is the primary calendar where the event is stored and cannot be modified without appropriate permissions. Changing this would require moving the event to a different calendar

Show child attributes

Update meeting details in calendar

cURL

Copy

Ask AI

```
curl --request PATCH \
  --url https://api.cal.com/v2/calendars/{calendar}/events/{eventUid} \
  --header 'Authorization: <authorization>' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
  "start": {
    "time": "2023-11-07T05:31:56Z",
    "timeZone": "<string>"
  },
  "end": {
    "time": "2023-11-07T05:31:56Z",
    "timeZone": "<string>"
  },

}'
```

`pending`,

`declined`,

boolean \| null

optional

boolean \| null

host

boolean \| null

Indicates if this attendee is the host

Copy

Ask AI

```
curl --request POST \
```
```
  --url https://api.cal.com/v2/event-types/{eventTypeId}/webhooks \
  --header 'Authorization: <authorization>' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
  "payloadTemplate": "{\"content\":\"A new event has been scheduled\",\"type\":\"{{type}}\",\"name\":\"{{title}}\",\"organizer\":\"{{organizer.name}}\",\"booker\":\"{{attendees.0.name}}\"}",
  "active": true,
  "subscriberUrl": "<string>",
  "triggers": [\
    "BOOKING_CREATED",\
    "BOOKING_RESCHEDULED",\
    "BOOKING_CANCELLED",\
    "BOOKING_CONFIRMED",\
    "BOOKING_REJECTED",\
    "BOOKING_COMPLETED",\
    "BOOKING_NO_SHOW",\
    "BOOKING_REOPENED"\
  ],
  "secret": "<string>"
}'
```

#### Headers

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types-webhooks/create-a-webhook#parameter-authorization)

Authorization

string

required

value must be `Bearer <token>` where `<token>` is api key prefixed with cal\_ or managed user access token

#### Path Parameters

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types-webhooks/create-a-webhook#parameter-event-type-id)

eventTypeId

number

required

#### Body

application/json

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types-webhooks/create-a-webhook#body-active)

active

boolean

required

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types-webhooks/create-a-webhook#body-subscriber-url)

subscriberUrl

string

required

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types-webhooks/create-a-webhook#body-triggers)

triggers

enum<string>

required

Available options:

`BOOKING_CREATED`,

`BOOKING_PAYMENT_INITIATED`,

`BOOKING_PAID`,

`BOOKING_RESCHEDULED`,

`BOOKING_REQUESTED`,

`BOOKING_CANCELLED`,

`BOOKING_REJECTED`,

`BOOKING_NO_SHOW_UPDATED`,

`FORM_SUBMITTED`,

`MEETING_ENDED`,

`MEETING_STARTED`,

`RECORDING_READY`,

`INSTANT_MEETING`,

`RECORDING_TRANSCRIPTION_GENERATED`,

`OOO_CREATED`,

`AFTER_HOSTS_CAL_VIDEO_NO_SHOW`,

`AFTER_GUESTS_CAL_VIDEO_NO_SHOW`,

`FORM_SUBMITTED_NO_EVENT`

Example:

```
[\
  "BOOKING_CREATED",\
  "BOOKING_RESCHEDULED",\
  "BOOKING_CANCELLED",\
  "BOOKING_CONFIRMED",\
  "BOOKING_REJECTED",\
  "BOOKING_COMPLETED",\
  "BOOKING_NO_SHOW",\
  "BOOKING_REOPENED"\
]
```

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types-webhooks/create-a-webhook#body-payload-template)

payloadTemplate

string

The template of the payload that will be sent to the subscriberUrl, check cal.com/docs/core-features/webhooks for more information

Example:

`"{\"content\":\"A new event has been scheduled\",\"type\":\"{{type}}\",\"name\":\"{{title}}\",\"organizer\":\"{{organizer.name}}\",\"booker\":\"{{attendees.0.name}}\"}"`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types-webhooks/create-a-webhook#body-secret)

secret

string

#### Headers

cal-api-version

string

Authorization

string

#### Body

application/json

required

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/create-an-event-type#body-length-in-minutes-options)

lengthInMinutesOptions

string\[\]

If you want that user can choose between different lengths of the event you can specify them here. Must include the provided `lengthInMinutes`.

Example:

```

```

string

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/create-an-event-type#body-booking-fields)

bookingFields

object\[\]

Custom fields that can be added to the booking form when the event is booked by someone. By default booking form has name and email field.

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/create-an-event-type#body-booking-fields-type)

type

string

required

only allowed value for type is `name`. Used for having 1 booking field for both first name and last name.

Example:

`"name"`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/create-an-event-type#body-booking-fields-label)

label

string

required

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/create-an-event-type#body-booking-fields-placeholder)

placeholder

string

required

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/create-an-event-type#body-booking-fields-disable-on-prefill)

disableOnPrefill

boolean

Disable this booking field if the URL contains query parameter with key equal to the slug and prefill it with the provided value. For example, if URL contains query parameter `&name=bob`, the name field will be prefilled with this value and disabled. In case of Booker atom need to pass 'name' to defaultFormValues prop with the desired value e.g. `defaultFormValues={{name: 'bob'}}`. See guide [https://cal.com/docs/platform/guides/booking-fields](https://cal.com/docs/platform/guides/booking-fields)

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/create-an-event-type#body-disable-guests)

disableGuests

boolean

If true, person booking this event can't add guests via their emails.

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/create-an-event-type#body-slot-interval)

slotInterval

number

Number representing length of each slot when event is booked. By default it equal length of the event type.
If event length is 60 minutes then we would have slots 9AM, 10AM, 11AM etc. but if it was changed to 30 minutes then
we would have slots 9AM, 9:30AM, 10AM, 10:30AM etc. as the available times to book the 60 minute event.

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/create-an-event-type#body-minimum-booking-notice)

minimumBookingNotice

number

Minimum number of minutes before the event that a booking can be made.

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/create-an-event-type#body-before-event-buffer)

beforeEventBuffer

number

Time spaces that can be prepended before an event to give more time before it.

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/create-an-event-type#body-after-event-buffer)

afterEventBuffer

number

Time spaces that can be appended after an event to give more time after it.

Show child attributes

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/create-an-event-type#body-booking-window-type)

bookingWindow.type

enum<string>

required

Whether the window should be business days, calendar days or a range of dates

Available options:

`businessDays`,

`calendarDays`,

`range`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/create-an-event-type#body-booking-window-value)

bookingWindow.value

number

required

How many business day into the future can this event be booked

Example:

`5`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/create-an-event-type#body-booking-window-rolling)

bookingWindow.rolling

boolean

```
Determines the behavior of the booking window:
  - If **true**, the window is rolling. This means the number of available days will always be equal the specified 'value'
    and adjust dynamically as bookings are made. For example, if 'value' is 3 and availability is only on Mondays,
    a booker attempting to schedule on November 10 will see slots on November 11, 18, and 25. As one of these days
    becomes fully booked, a new day (e.g., December 2) will open up to ensure 3 available days are always visible.
  - If **false**, the window is fixed. This means the booking window only considers the next 'value' days from the
    moment someone is trying to book. For example, if 'value' is 3, availability is only on Mondays, and the current
    date is November 10, the booker will only see slots on November 11 because the window is restricted to the next
    3 calendar days (November 10–12).
```

Example:

`true`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/create-an-event-type#body-offset-start)

number

Delete an event type

cURL

Copy

Ask AI

```
curl --request DELETE \
  --url https://api.cal.com/v2/event-types/{eventTypeId} \
  --header 'Authorization: <authorization>' \
  --header 'cal-api-version: <cal-api-version>'
```

```
curl --request DELETE \
  --url https://api.cal.com/v2/event-types/{eventTypeId} \
```

200

Copy

Ask AI

```
{
  "status": "success",
  "data": {
    "id": 1,
    "lengthInMinutes": 60,
    "title": "Learn the secrets of masterchief!",
    "slug": "<string>"
  }
}
```

#### Headers

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/delete-an-event-type#parameter-cal-api-version)

cal-api-version

string

default:2024-06-14

required

Must be set to 2024-06-14

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/delete-an-event-type#parameter-authorization)

Authorization

string

required

value must be `Bearer <token>` where `<token>` is api key prefixed with cal\_ or managed user access token

#### Path Parameters

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/delete-an-event-type#parameter-event-type-id)

eventTypeId

number

required

#### Response

200 - application/json

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/delete-an-event-type#response-status)

status

enum<string>

required

Available options:

`success`,

`error`

Example:

`"success"`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/delete-an-event-type#response-data)

data

object

required

data.id

number

required

Example:

`1`

data.lengthInMinutes

number

required

Example:

`60`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/delete-an-event-type#response-data-title)

data.title

string

required

Example:

`"Learn the secrets of masterchief!"`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/delete-an-event-type#response-data-slug)

data.slug

string

required

#### Headers

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/get-all-event-types#parameter-cal-api-version)

cal-api-version

string

default:2024-06-14

required

Must be set to 2024-06-14

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/get-all-event-types#parameter-authorization)

Authorization

string

value must be `Bearer <token>` where `<token>` is api key prefixed with cal\_ or managed user access token

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/get-all-event-types#parameter-x-cal-secret-key)

x-cal-secret-key

string

For platform customers - OAuth client secret key

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/get-all-event-types#parameter-x-cal-client-id)

x-cal-client-id

string

For platform customers - OAuth client ID

#### Query Parameters

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/get-all-event-types#parameter-username)

username

string

The username of the user to get event types for. If only username provided will get all event types.

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/get-all-event-types#parameter-event-slug)

eventSlug

string

Slug of event type to return. Notably, if eventSlug is provided then username must be provided too, because multiple users can have event with same slug.

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/get-all-event-types#parameter-usernames)

usernames

string

Get dynamic event type for multiple usernames separated by comma. e.g `usernames=alice,bob`

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/get-all-event-types#parameter-org-slug)

orgSlug

string

slug of the user's organization if he is in one, orgId is not required if using this parameter

[​](https://cal.com/docs/api-reference/v2/event-types/get-all-event-types#parameter-org-id)

orgId

number

ID of the organization of the user you want the get the event-types of, orgSlug is not needed when using this parameter
